title: Hamzah, lion of Allah
hook: his uncle Hamzah, the lion of Allah, is killed at Uhud, and the Prophet ﷺ grieves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uhud, and the archers who left too soon. Your line was hold the hill. Did you finish the thing you wanted to leave early? Day two hundred sixty-seven.

Years before Medina, back in Mecca, a big, proud hunter comes home from the desert with his bow on his shoulder. A woman stops him: while you were gone, Abu Jahl insulted your nephew Muhammad to his face, and he said nothing back. The hunter turns around, walks straight into the gathering of Quraysh, finds Abu Jahl, and strikes him with his bow. Then he says, in front of everyone: I follow his religion too. Hit me back if you can. That was Hamzah, uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and from that day, the biographers say, Quraysh thought twice about harming the Prophet. Today, the man they called the lion of God.
screen: `A HUNTER COMES HOME.` → `HE STRIKES ABU JAHL.` → `I FOLLOW HIS RELIGION TOO.`

segments.voice: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was the Prophet's uncle, but the biographers say close to him in age, and the two had been nursed by the same woman as babies. The Prophet called him his brother through nursing. He was strong, fearless, and at Badr he fought at the front. People called him asad Allah, the lion of God. But at Uhud there was a man watching for him. Wahshi was an Abyssinian slave in Mecca, skilled with a short throwing spear. His master had promised him his freedom if he killed Hamzah, whose sword had killed the master's uncle at Badr. Wahshi told the story himself, years later, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. He hid behind a rock, waited for Hamzah to pass, and threw. Hamzah fell. After the battle, his body was found mutilated. The early biographers describe the Prophet standing over him in deep grief. Back in Medina, he heard the women of the Ansar weeping for their dead, and he said: but Hamzah has no women to weep for him. And the women of Medina came to his door to weep for Hamzah. Tradition calls Hamzah the master of the martyrs, and his grave lies at the foot of Uhud. And here is the part that's hardest. Years later, Wahshi became Muslim and came to the Prophet. The Prophet did not turn him away. Bukhari says he asked one question: are you the one who killed Hamzah? Wahshi said it was as he'd been told. And then the Prophet said: can you keep your face out of my sight? He accepted him. He still grieved. Both were true.
screen: `ASAD ALLAH — THE LION OF GOD.` · `WAHSHI BEHIND THE ROCK.` · `NO ONE TO WEEP FOR HAMZAH.` · `ACCEPTED, AND STILL GRIEVED.` · then, large: `THE LION FELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone brave. Sit, and let a person come to mind who stood up when it cost them something. It could be someone famous, or someone only you know: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who spoke up for you in a room where nobody else would. If they've died, let yourself miss them for a minute, the way the Prophet missed Hamzah. If you pray, you can make du'a for them. The bell holds the time.
Hamzah. The Prophet's uncle and nursing brother, the lion of God, killed at Uhud and remembered as the master of the martyrs. Today's word.
Your line: the lion fell. Today, tell someone about the brave person you remembered, so they're honored out loud. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to Medina visit the graves of Hamzah and the martyrs of Uhud at the foot of the mountain, greeting them and praying for them, and many Muslims name their sons Hamzah.

fork.setup: years after Uhud, the man who killed your uncle comes to you and becomes Muslim. what do you do?
options: accept him, and ask him to keep out of your sight.
embrace him as if nothing happened.
fork.reveal: the Prophet accepted him, asked one question, then said: can you keep your face out of my sight? acceptance, and grief, both.

original.note: Arabic: the lion of God, the title given to Hamzah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a war hero.
what it means: the Prophet's uncle and nursing brother, killed at Uhud, whose death the Prophet grieved openly and whose killer he accepted.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 4072 is Wahshi's own account; the title sayyid ash-shuhada' comes from reports in al-Hakim and others.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4072 (Wahshi's account of Hamzah's death and his meeting with the Prophet)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2645 (Hamzah, the Prophet's brother through nursing)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1591 (but Hamzah has no women to weep for him)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): Hamzah's conversion; the Prophet's grief

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: Bukhari 4072 has the Prophet ask Wahshi one question, not hear the whole story, and does not say 'I forgive you', so the ending now says he accepted him and still grieved (teach, head, myth, fork, trapdoor); Hamzah's age and the Prophet's grief attributed to the biographers; 'Muslims call' became 'tradition calls'.
Hamzah's conversion story (striking Abu Jahl) follows Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
The mutilation is mentioned but not described, and Hind bint 'Utbah is not named (she later became Muslim). Keeper to confirm that level of detail.
Weeping for the dead: later hadith restrict wailing; the Ibn Majah report is told as it stands. Confirm tone.
'Master of the martyrs' (sayyid ash-shuhada') sourced to al-Hakim and others; confirm.
